title: Authenticity: choosing what your yoga or fitness brand is true to
audience: Yoga, Pilates and personal or group fitness teachers who are naming, describing or promoting their own classes or services.
learningOutcomes: Describe the two kinds of authenticity a teaching brand can rest on: fidelity to a tradition, and honesty about personal practice
Choose the kind that fits your training and your intended clients, and state it in one plain sentence
Check each brand claim against what happens in your class, and record the evidence for it

instruction.heading: Authenticity is a promise about what is real
instruction.body: Clients use the word authentic to mean that a teacher is what they appear to be. In a yoga or fitness business, that realness can come from two places. The first is a tradition: a named style, its history, its vocabulary, and a discipline the teacher has been trained in and can describe in their own words. The second is the teacher's personal practice: why they teach, what their body has taught them, and what they actually do with a room of people. Neither source is automatically better. They attract different people, and a brand that claims both without choosing can look muddled. Before you write any public description, decide which source your teaching draws on most, and be ready to explain how it does so.

instruction.heading: Matching the kind of authenticity to the client
instruction.body: A teacher who trains in a set method and teaches it closely will usually attract clients who value rigour, a consistent sequence and a clear line back to the source. Those clients ask about training and notice shortcuts. A teacher who builds classes from several disciplines, and who speaks openly about their own path, tends to attract clients who want approachable, adaptable sessions and a relationship with the teacher. Those clients respond to honesty and to being invited in. Problems start when the two are mixed without intent. A class that presents itself as strictly traditional, but changes the sequence each week and plays loud music, will lose the traditional clients and look like a gimmick to everyone else. Choose a primary source, let any secondary influences sit beside it openly, and say so.

instruction.heading: Turning a claim into something you can show
instruction.body: Words such as traditional, authentic, certified, lineage and original carry weight with clients, so each one needs evidence behind it. Keep the training certificate, the course record, the dates the work was completed, and a written account of any lineage you describe, including who taught you and what they taught you. If you cannot name the source of a term, do not use the term. Treat each one as a claim that must be true and provable, because consumer law may treat a misleading description of a service as a problem. Check the current Australian consumer law position before you rely on this point.

instruction.heading: Keeping the promise consistent across every channel
instruction.body: A brand is what the client experiences from the first search result to the last class. Your website, your timetable, your social posts, your bio and the words you use at the start of a class should describe the same teacher and the same method. Use the business name held as {{business:business.display_name}} on every channel so that clients can find one consistent offer. Read each channel side by side. If the website calls the class gentle and the class itself is intense, the gap will show. Ask a client who has attended for about three months to describe your class in their own words, and compare that answer with your written description. Where the two differ, change the description or change the class, and record which one you chose and why.

procedure: Write down the source your teaching draws on most, and one secondary source if you have one
Write one plain sentence that says who the class is for and which kind of authenticity it rests on
List every public claim you make about training, lineage, style or results
For each claim, attach the evidence that shows it is true, and remove any claim that has no evidence
Compare your website, timetable, bio and in-class wording, and align them with the sentence from step two
Ask one recent client to describe the class in their own words, and note any gap
Record the statement, the claim list, the evidence references and the date of the review

workedExamples.situation: A fictional teacher, Dana, runs a morning Pilates class in Bendigo. Her website says 'classical method' and 'traditional reformer work', but she trained in a modern mat-based program and adds music and new exercises most weeks.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which of Dana's claims should she keep, and what should she change?
workedExamples.reasoning: She should keep only the claims she can evidence. She holds no classical training record, so 'classical method' has to go. Her real source is the modern mat-based program, which is an honest and marketable base. She should name that source, describe the music and new exercises as her own additions, and file the training evidence she holds. Clients who want approachable, adaptable sessions will then know what they are getting, and the traditional-minded clients will not be misled.

workedExamples.situation: A new teacher, Leilani, is told by a friend that her Hatha classes would sound 'more authentic' if she mentioned a teacher she has never trained with.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should she name that teacher on her website?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. She cannot evidence a training relationship that does not exist, and naming a teacher who never taught her misrepresents her lineage. She should name the teachers she has actually trained with, state the length and nature of her training, and describe her classes in plain language. If she later completes training under a named teacher, she can add that with the evidence in hand.

equipmentAndPpe: No PPE is required for this lesson
Training certificates and course records, kept in one folder
Current website, timetable, bio and social profile text, saved for side-by-side review
A notebook or document for the claim list and the review date

commonErrors.error: Mixing two sources of authenticity without deciding which one leads
commonErrors.prevention: Choose one primary source and write one sentence that states it. Let any secondary influences sit beside it openly.

commonErrors.error: Using a tradition's vocabulary as decoration
commonErrors.prevention: Use a term only when you can name its source and explain how your class relates to it.

commonErrors.error: Publishing claims that the class has never been tested against
commonErrors.prevention: Ask a recent client to describe the class, and compare the answer with your public description before you change anything.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Claims about curing, treating or preventing a health condition can be regulated in Australia. Do not make such claims until they have been checked.
Consumer law may apply to advertising claims about training, style or results.

qualityStandard: Every public claim about training, lineage or results has a named piece of evidence held by the business
The brand sentence matches the website, timetable, bio and in-class wording
Each term that cannot be evidenced has been removed, or is labelled as the teacher's own description
documentationEvidence: Brand sentence, with the date it was written
Claim list with an evidence reference for each claim
Side-by-side review record, including the client description used for comparison
summary: Authenticity can rest on a tradition, on personal practice, or on a deliberate mix of both
Choose one primary source and state it plainly, because mixing sources without intent erodes trust
Every claim needs evidence you hold, and any claim you cannot show should be removed
Keep the same description on every channel, and check it with a real client

knowledgeChecks.question: A teacher wants to describe a class as rooted in a specific tradition. What must be true first?
options: The class must use the tradition's music
The teacher can name the source and explain how the class relates to it
The website must state that the price is lower than the tradition's usual price

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is mixing two sources of authenticity without a decision a risk?
options: Clients who want rigour and clients who want adaptability may both lose trust in a brand that is unclear
The class becomes unlawful in every Australian state if the teacher uses two sources at once
It guarantees that no client will ask about training and removes the need for any records

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about a lineage claim is correct?
options: If the teacher holds any certificate, any lineage can be claimed and the claim can go on the website
A lineage is decided by how many people follow the teacher online and the number of likes on each post
A lineage claim should be backed by a record of who trained the teacher and what they taught
